## **Design**
<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-primary">

:bulb: **Tip:** The `.puml` files used to create diagrams are in `docs/diagrams`. Refer to the [_PlantUML Tutorial_ at se-edu/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/plantUml.html) to learn how to create and edit diagrams.
### Architecture
The ***Architecture Diagram*** given above explains the high-level design of the App.
The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.
**Main components of the architecture**

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`UI`**](#ui-component): The UI of the App.
* [**`Logic`**](#logic-component): The command executor.
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
### UI component
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)
![Structure of the UI Component](images/UiClassDiagram.png)

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts, such as `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`, and `StatusBarFooter`. All of these, including `MainWindow`, inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
The `UI` component,
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Person` objects from the model.
#### Command input and recall

`CommandBox` owns one package-private `CommandHistory` for its lifetime. This helper is UI state rather than member data: it stores at most 100 exact nonblank submissions, including duplicates and failures, and is never persisted. Oldest entries are evicted when the capacity is reached. The UI class diagram focuses on visible components; this internal helper does not extend `UiPart`.

`CommandHistory` keeps a cursor between the oldest entry and a position just after the newest entry. Up from the latter position captures the current input as a draft, then visits older entries. Down visits newer entries and restores the draft when the cursor reaches the end. Boundaries do not wrap. An edit or new submission resets navigation to the end without changing previously recorded text.

`CommandBox` filters unmodified Up/Down key presses on its text field. Programmatic recall uses `isRecallingHistory` so the existing text-change listener clears error styling without resetting the browsing cursor. User edits reset the cursor, making an edited recall a new draft. Replacing text positions the caret at the end. Enter records the nonblank input before calling the executor, so parsing and execution failures can both be recalled. Existing success clearing and failure feedback remain in place. Browsing never calls the executor or changes the address book's undo/redo history.

`CommandHistoryTest` tests the bounded state machine without JavaFX. `CommandBoxTest` dispatches keyboard and action events through the real FXML text field with a recording executor, covering draft restoration, edited recalls, modifiers, failed submissions and independent histories. Like `PersonCardTest`, the graphical class requires a graphical session and `HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true`:
```sh
./gradlew test --tests seedu.address.ui.CommandHistoryTest
HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true ./gradlew test --tests seedu.address.ui.CommandBoxTest --rerun-tasks

On Windows PowerShell, set `$env:HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS = "true"` before running the corresponding `./gradlew.bat` command. Without this variable, only the graphical class is skipped; the history state-machine tests still run in ordinary CI.
#### Member cards

`PersonListPanel` observes the filtered and sorted person view exposed by `Logic`. Its list cells create a `PersonCard` for each displayed person, passing the cell's one-based index. When `find`, `filter`, `sort`, or `list` changes the displayed results, the list updates the cards and their indices. The existing UI class diagram shows this relationship; the card enhancement adds no new classes or dependencies.

`PersonCard` loads `PersonListCard.fxml` through `UiPart`. The FXML `fx:id` attributes match the controller's `@FXML` fields. The constructor reads the person's public getters to populate the name, contact details, membership status, member type, optional role, and instruments. Type and status appear as text badges. `PersonCard.toDisplayText` capitalises the first character and replaces keyword hyphens with spaces for display (for example, `active-alumnus` becomes `Active alumnus`); model values, command keywords and storage remain unchanged. Card-specific styles in `DarkTheme.css` distinguish the name heading, contact details, secondary information and badges without changing the rest of the theme. Instrument labels use `Instrument.toDisplayString()` and are sorted by name, ignoring case.

When no role is recorded, the role label has both `visible` and `managed` set to `false`: it is hidden and does not reserve layout space. Name, contact, and role labels allow text wrapping, while flow panes allow the membership details and instrument labels to move onto additional rows as space narrows. These changes affect presentation only; the model and stored records are unchanged.

`PersonCardTest` loads the actual FXML and checks field values, all status/type combinations, role visibility and layout participation, empty instruments, and instrument ordering. It runs on the JavaFX application thread and requires a working graphical session. Enable it with the environment variable `HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true`; otherwise JUnit skips this test class so the existing headless CI remains usable. On Linux/macOS, run:
```sh
HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true ./gradlew test --tests seedu.address.ui.PersonCardTest --rerun-tasks

On Windows PowerShell, set `$env:HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS = "true"` and run `./gradlew.bat test --tests seedu.address.ui.PersonCardTest --rerun-tasks`. These tests do not replace visual checks for wrapping and scrolling; use the member-card scenarios in the manual-testing section below.
#### Empty member lists

`MainWindow` supplies the displayed list and the full directory through `Logic.getPersonList()` to `PersonListPanel`. A wrapped `ListView` placeholder binds its guidance to whether the full directory is empty; `ListView` controls its visibility from the displayed list. Observing the full list prevents stale guidance when a nonmatching record is removed or the directory is reset while no results are shown. The placeholder width follows the list viewport. `PersonListPanelEmptyStateTest` exercises both states, model transitions, and narrow rendering with `HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true`.
#### Member result count

`Logic.getPersonList()` exposes the address book's unmodifiable observable full list. `MainWindow` supplies this and the filtered/sorted list to `PersonListPanel`. The result-count label binds to both lists, so a change to the total updates the label even if the displayed results stay unchanged. The full-list view stays live across resets, imports, undo/redo, and save-failure rollback. `PersonListPanelCountTest` exercises these observable updates and narrow layout with `HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true`.
#### Command feedback

`MainWindow` passes `FeedbackType.SUCCESS` after `Logic.execute` returns and `FeedbackType.ERROR` for `CommandException` or `ParseException`, including save failures. Startup notices use `INFORMATION`. `ResultDisplay` preserves the message text, sets an explicit outcome label and CSS class, and resets the scroll position for each message. The read-only `TextArea` wraps text and retains vertical scrolling and selection. `ResultDisplayTest` checks the rendered FXML, outcome transitions, narrow layout, and command routing with a storage failure. Enable these graphical tests with `HIVEMIND_UI_TESTS=true`.
### Logic component
**API** : [`Logic.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/logic/Logic.java)
Here's a (partial) class diagram of the `Logic` component:
The sequence diagram below illustrates the interactions within the `Logic` component, taking `execute("delete 1")` API call as an example.
![Interactions Inside the Logic Component for the `delete 1` Command](images/DeleteSequenceDiagram.png)

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** The lifeline for `DeleteCommandParser` should end at the destroy marker (X), but due to a limitation of PlantUML, it continues to the end of the diagram.
How the `Logic` component works:

1. When `Logic` is called upon to execute a command, the command is passed to an `AddressBookParser` object, which in turn creates a parser that matches the command (e.g., `DeleteCommandParser`) and uses it to parse the command.
1. This results in a `Command` object (more precisely, an object of one of its subclasses e.g., `DeleteCommand`) which is executed by the `LogicManager`.
1. The command can communicate with the `Model` when it is executed (e.g. to delete a person).
Note that although this is shown as a single step in the diagram above for simplicity, the code can require several interactions between the command object and the `Model` to complete the operation.
1. The result of the command execution is encapsulated as a `CommandResult` object which is returned from `Logic`.

The parser class diagram below uses `add` as one example of how HiveMind parses commands. It focuses on the Logic parser classes; the member fields are described in the text below rather than drawing the Model classes here:
How the parsing works:
* `AddressBookParser` creates an `AddCommandParser` for `add`. The parser tokenizes prefixes into an `ArgumentMultimap` and checks that `n/`, `p/`, `e/`, and `s/` are present.

* `ParserUtil` validates the status, member type, optional role, instruments, and participation groups. When `ty/` is omitted, `AddCommandParser` uses `student`; when `r/` is omitted, the person's role is empty. Repeated `g/` prefixes add groups to the person's group set.
* `AddCommandParser` creates a `Person` from the parsed values, then an `AddCommand` containing that person. `AddressBookParser` returns it as a `Command` to `LogicManager`.
* Other command parsers follow the same `Parser` interface, although their accepted prefixes and validation rules differ.
### Model component
**API** : [`Model.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/model/Model.java)
The `Model` component,
* stores the address book data i.e., all `Person` objects (which are contained in a `UniquePersonList` object).

* maintains a `FilteredList<Person>` view of the directory and a `SortedList<Person>` view of those filtered results. It exposes the sorted view as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when membership or ordering changes.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)
### Storage component
**API** : [`Storage.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/storage/Storage.java)
The `Storage` component,
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which delegates the actual JSON file access to `JsonAddressBookStorage` and `JsonUserPrefsStorage` (one class per data file).
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)

`JsonAdaptedPerson` rejects null group entries and names for which `String.isBlank()` returns true. For each remaining entry, it skips the membership if `Group.isValidName()` returns false. This omits Unicode-whitespace-only names such as `"\u00A0"` while preserving the person and valid groups. Valid names are constructed as `Group` objects, which replace runs of Unicode whitespace with one ordinary space and trim the result.

`JsonAdaptedPerson` also skips instrument entries whose names are not blank according to `String.isBlank()` but normalize to empty. Remaining instrument names are compared ignoring case and normalized Unicode whitespace. If old entries collapse to the same instrument name, the loader keeps the highest years of experience. These migrations preserve the member's record ID and other fields; loading does not rewrite the file.

This loading rule applies only to saved JSON data. Command parsing rejects every group name that normalizes to empty. Loading does not rewrite the data file, and successfully loaded records remain editable and saveable. The next successful command requiring a save writes the directory without the skipped memberships.
### Common classes
Classes used by multiple components are in the `seedu.address.commons` package.
## **Implementation**
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
### Application file locations
`ApplicationPaths` provides one application home for every file owned by HiveMind. In a packaged launch, it converts
the application code-source URI to a `Path`, resolves the canonical JAR location, and uses the JAR's parent directory.
Converting the URI through `Path.of(URI)` preserves spaces and non-ASCII characters correctly. In a development or
test launch, where the code source is a classes directory rather than a packaged file, it retains the normalized
working directory for compatibility with Gradle and IDE launches.
`LogsCenter` obtains its log path from `ApplicationPaths` during its initial static configuration, before the first
application log entry can create a file. `MainApp` uses the same abstraction for preferences, member data and the
imports directory. `ImportCommand` and `ExportCommand` use it for their default directories. Recovery backups remain
beside the configured member-data file, so they are under the same application home. Tests can continue to pass
explicit temporary import and export directories to the commands, avoiding writes to the repository during unit and
integration testing.
`ApplicationPathsTest` covers packaged paths containing spaces and non-ASCII characters, the development-launch
fallback, and confinement of every configured application path under the shared home directory. The packaged-JAR
manual test below verifies the startup and command paths together from a different working directory.
### Adding members and record identity

`AddCommandParser` validates the required name, phone, email and status, defaults an omitted type to `student`, and constructs a `Person`. `Name` accepts Unicode letters, combining accents and numbers, ordinary spaces, apostrophes, hyphens and full stops; the first character must be a letter or number. A `/` is valid only within the standalone markers `s/o` and `d/o` (ASCII, any case) between two name parts, so legal names such as `Ravi s/o Kumar` can be stored. Any other `/` remains invalid, so a mistyped prefix such as `ph/` in a name value is still rejected instead of being saved as part of the name. Neither marker can be a mistyped prefix: no command uses `d/`, and no status starts with `o`. Markers such as `a/l` are deliberately excluded, as `a/` is the removed address prefix. A lowercase `s/o` in a command is still tokenized as the status prefix; the User Guide asks users to type `S/O`, which `ArgumentTokenizer` keeps as text because it is a wrong-case prefix after the first accepted prefix.

`AddCommand` checks the complete directory for a case-insensitive name match or an exact phone-number match. It adds a warning line for each matching record and still adds the new member, as specified by UC01. `LogicManager` saves the resulting directory before returning the warnings and success message; its existing rollback restores the directory if saving fails.

Each `Person` has a stable UUID record ID, independent of editable contact details. `Person.isSamePerson` compares IDs, while `Person.equals` compares recorded details for snapshot and CSV data comparisons. `UniquePersonList` checks, replaces and removes records by ID. `EditCommand` retains the selected person's ID, so identical names or even identical details never make an edit or deletion target another record. Sorting caches source positions by ID for the same reason.

`JsonAdaptedPerson` saves the ID with the other fields and restores it on load. Older files without IDs receive fresh IDs as they load, which are written on the next successful data change. Malformed or repeated IDs are invalid data. Undo snapshots retain the same IDs because they copy the immutable person records.

**Design choice:** Record IDs allow legitimate shared names and phone numbers without treating editable contact details as permanent identity. They add one internal JSON field but require no new user command or confirmation step. CSV keeps its existing eight columns and receives new record IDs on import. Since CSV has no IDs, `ImportCommand` rejects records with identical recorded details against the existing directory or earlier CSV rows, while allowing shared names with differing details.
### Participation groups

`Group` stores a non-blank name and normalizes whitespace before comparing names ignoring case. `ParserUtil.parseGroups` builds a set, so repeating `g/Choir g/choir` records one group. `add` may omit all groups. `edit` preserves groups unless `g/` is supplied; named groups replace the entire set, and a single empty `g/` clears it. An empty value mixed with named groups is rejected.

For older JSON files, `JsonAdaptedPerson` omits a Unicode-space-only group that earlier versions accepted, preserving the member and its remaining groups. New commands still reject such blank group names; null and previously invalid blank JSON group entries remain invalid data.

`Person` keeps a defensive copy of its group set and exposes an unmodifiable view. JSON saves group names and defaults a missing groups field to an empty set for older files. `PersonCard` renders sorted group names as separate, wrapping labels below a `Groups:` heading. The whole section is hidden and unmanaged when empty. This keeps a group containing a comma distinguishable from multiple groups. Instrument and group badges are constrained to their flow pane's width, and list cells follow the viewport width so long values wrap within the card.
### Partial-name search

The `find` command matches any part of a person's name, ignoring case. For example, `find ali` matches `Alice Tan`. Multiple whitespace-separated keywords use OR: a person is included when at least one keyword matches. Only the name is searched.

`FindCommandParser` rejects empty arguments and splits valid arguments into keywords. It constructs a `FindCommand` containing a `NameContainsKeywordsPredicate`. When executed, the command passes the predicate to `ModelManager.updateFilteredPersonList`, which updates the predicate of the JavaFX `FilteredList`. The UI observes the wrapping `SortedList` and displays the matching persons in the selected order with indices starting at 1; the underlying address book remains unchanged.
The following two sequence diagrams trace a successful `find ali` command. Parsing and execution are shown separately so the labels remain readable at the guide's width.
First, `LogicManager` calls `AddressBookParser.parseCommand`, which returns the parsed command `f` after creating its predicate `p`.
![Find command parsing: keyword parsing, predicate creation, and command creation](images/FindParsingSequenceDiagram.png)

Execution then continues in `LogicManager`. The participant `m:Model` is implemented by `ModelManager`, and `p:Predicate` is the `NameContainsKeywordsPredicate` created during parsing. Setting the predicate evaluates the full directory, replacing any previous search or filter. The command uses the resulting list size for its feedback message and does not require a save. UI list-change notifications are omitted.
![Find command execution: predicate evaluation, result count, and feedback](images/FindSequenceDiagram.png)

`NameContainsKeywordsPredicate` uses `StringUtil.containsSubstringIgnoreCase` for each keyword. The helper trims the keyword, rejects null, empty or multiple-word inputs, and normalises both strings with `Locale.ROOT` before checking for a substring. The original `containsWordIgnoreCase` helper retains its whole-word behaviour for other callers.

Tests in `StringUtilTest` cover substring positions, case differences, invalid inputs and non-matches. `NameContainsKeywordsPredicateTest` verifies name-only matching and OR semantics. `FindCommandTest` checks the resulting persons and feedback count, while `FindCommandParserTest` covers empty arguments and extra whitespace.
### Sorting displayed members

`SortCommandParser` accepts exactly one attribute, `name` or `status`, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. `SortCommandParser` maps each keyword to a `SortKey` enum value holding its comparator. `SortCommand` passes that comparator to `Model.updateSortedPersonList`. Name sorting compares full names using `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`. Status sorting uses explicit ranks: `MEMBER`, `ACTIVE_ALUMNUS`, then `INACTIVE_ALUMNUS`, independently of enum declaration order.

`ModelManager` wraps its `FilteredList<Person>` in a `SortedList<Person>`. `getFilteredPersonList` exposes this sorted view to the UI and index-based commands, keeping displayed indices consistent with edit and delete. The model breaks comparator ties using cached directory positions keyed by record ID, so switching from name sorting still restores directory order within each status, including members with identical details. A source-list listener refreshes the cache before the filtered and sorted views process each directory change; comparisons use constant-time lookups. Stored records are not reordered, and `SortCommand.requiresSave` returns false.

Find/filter update the predicate without clearing the comparator. Add/edit retain sorting while restoring the full directory. `ListCommand` resets the predicate and clears the comparator to restore insertion order. A new model starts without a comparator, so sorting is session-only.

Sorting tests cover case-insensitive names, membership order, ties, switching ordering, filter/search transitions, empty results, list reset, add/edit/delete interactions and unchanged stored order. Parser tests cover case and whitespace, missing attributes, unsupported attributes and extra arguments.
### Status, instrument, type, role, and group filtering

`FilterCommandParser` accepts repeated `s/STATUS`, `i/NAME[:MIN_YEARS]`, `ty/TYPE`, `r/ROLE`, and `g/GROUP` arguments and requires at least one criterion. It validates statuses, member types, and roles through `ParserUtil.parseStatus`, `parseMemberType`, and `parseRole`. Groups use `ParserUtil.parseGroups`, reusing the same validation and deduplication as `add` and `edit`. Its `parseInstrumentCriterion` helper validates names through `ParserUtil.parseInstrumentName` and optional whole minimum years from 0 to 99. Name-only criteria default to a minimum of zero. Invalid minimum years use `InstrumentCriterion.MESSAGE_MINIMUM_YEARS_CONSTRAINTS`.

Before tokenizing, the parser reuses `ArgumentTokenizer.verifyNoUnknownPrefixes` with its five accepted prefixes. This replaces the separate unsupported-prefix check: `n/`, `p/`, and `e/` receive specific errors, while removed and wrong-case prefixes are rejected only before the first accepted prefix, matching `edit`. Ambiguous slash text inside values remains literal to preserve valid free text; field validation then applies as usual.

`FilterCommand` stores immutable sets of statuses, `InstrumentCriterion` values, member types, roles, and groups. Each instrument criterion has a normalized `name` and an explicit `minimumYears`. Its `matches(Instrument)` method checks the whole name through `Instrument.hasName` and an inclusive experience threshold on the same recorded instrument. `Instrument` continues to represent actual years played in member records and storage. `PersonMatchesFilterPredicate` checks the selected statuses and member types and delegates instrument matching to each criterion. Roles match complete names, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace, without changing `Role.equals`. A missing role fails an explicit role criterion. Groups match any recorded participation group using `Group.equals`, which ignores case and extra whitespace while matching the whole name. People without groups fail an explicit group criterion. Criteria within a field use OR, including repeated names with different minimums, and different fields use AND. An omitted field imposes no restriction, so status-only filters also include matching people without instruments, roles, or groups.

The command replaces the predicate on the full directory's `FilteredList`, reports its match count, and leaves stored records unchanged. `list` restores all records. Parser, predicate, and command tests cover repeated criteria, invalid inputs, threshold boundaries, matching years on the correct instrument, combined criteria, people without instruments or groups, group-name normalization and whole-name matching, empty results, and searches after earlier filters.

The following two sequence diagrams trace a successful `filter s/member i/Violin:3 ty/teacher r/Conductor g/Chamber Orchestra` command. Parsing and execution are shown separately, as for `find`. In both diagrams, `criteria` is shorthand for the five sets of statuses, instrument criteria, member types, roles, and groups passed to the constructors.

First, `LogicManager` calls `AddressBookParser.parseCommand`, which delegates to `FilterCommandParser` to validate the criteria and return the parsed command `f`. No predicate is created during parsing.

[Open the parsing diagram at full size](images/FilterParsingSequenceDiagram.png). [PlantUML source](diagrams/FilterParsingSequenceDiagram.puml).

Execution then continues in `LogicManager`. The command creates the `PersonMatchesFilterPredicate` and applies it through `ModelManager.updateFilteredPersonList`. The participant `m:Model` is implemented by `ModelManager`, and `p:Predicate` is the predicate created during execution. Model snapshots and UI list-change notifications are omitted.
![Filter command execution: predicate creation, filtered-list evaluation, result count, and feedback](images/FilterSequenceDiagram.png)
[Open the execution diagram at full size](images/FilterSequenceDiagram.png). [PlantUML source](diagrams/FilterSequenceDiagram.puml).
### Exporting current results

`AddressBookParser` delegates `export [f/FIELD]...` to `ExportCommandParser`. With no arguments, the parser creates a default `ExportCommand` using `ExportField.DEFAULT_FIELDS`: name, phone, email, status, memberType, role, instruments, and groups. Otherwise, it tokenizes repeated `f/` values, matches their exact case-sensitive names against `ExportField` headers, and preserves the requested order. Unsupported, empty or repeated field selections and unexpected arguments cause a `ParseException` before execution, so no file is created.

`ExportCommand` stores an immutable copy of the selected fields. Its constructors reject empty selections and repeated fields with an `IllegalArgumentException`; null lists or entries cause a `NullPointerException`. When executed, it obtains the current results through `Model#getFilteredPersonList()`, which returns the filtered and sorted display view, and passes them to `CsvExporter.export(currentResults, exportDirectory, fields)`. Exporting does not update records or the display view. `requiresSave()` returns `false`, so `LogicManager` neither saves the address book nor changes undo/redo history.

`ExportField` defines each supported header and its value extractor. `CsvExporter` builds the header and each row from the same ordered selection. The existing two-argument `export(people, exportDirectory)` overload delegates to the full default selection. The three-argument overload also validates the selection before creating a file, protecting direct callers. Empty results produce only the selected headers. `CsvImporter` still requires the original eight headers in their original order, so partial exports and reordered full exports cannot be imported; the default export retains import compatibility.

Each exported value uses the existing CSV quoting and escaping: embedded quotation marks are doubled, and `CsvCellCodec` prefixes values that spreadsheet applications could interpret as formulas with a space. `ExportField` sorts instruments and groups by name, applies `CsvListCodec` to escape semicolons and backslashes within each list value, and joins the values with semicolons. `CsvImporter` decodes these escapes and removes the spreadsheet protection prefix when importing a compatible full export.

Before writing, `CsvExporter` finds the first unused filename in the form `current-results-XX.csv`, beginning with `current-results-01.csv`; existing exports are preserved rather than overwritten. `ExportCommand` logs successful exports at `INFO` with the row count, ordered columns and output path. If writing fails, it logs the row count, columns, export directory and exception stack trace at `WARNING`, then converts the `IOException` into a `CommandException`. These export outcome logs do not include member values or CSV contents.

`ExportCommandParserTest` and `AddressBookParserTest` cover default and selected-field commands and invalid syntax. `ExportCommandTest` covers constructor validation, results after `find`, `filter` and `sort`, empty results, immutable selections, and preservation of records and undo/redo history. `CsvExporterTest` covers selected column order, CSV quoting, list escaping, formula protection, empty results, and preservation of existing files and filename numbering. `CsvImporterTest` covers default export/import round trips and rejection of partial exports.

### Importing people from CSV

`AddressBookParser` routes `import FILE_NAME` to `ImportCommandParser`. The parser accepts a non-empty `.csv` file name without path separators, so `ImportCommand` always resolves it inside the `imports` directory.

`ImportCommand` asks `CsvImporter.importPeopleWithLineNumbers` to read the entire CSV before changing the model. `CsvImporter` validates the required header and eight-column layout, then constructs `Person` objects using the existing model value objects such as `Name`, `Phone`, `Email`, `Status`, and `MemberType`. This reuses the application's validation rules instead of duplicating them in the CSV layer. It returns the complete imported list with each record's starting physical line number only when every row is valid, including records spanning multiple lines.

After parsing succeeds, `ImportCommand` copies the current address book and checks every imported person's recorded details against the copy before adding it. This detects identical records against both existing members and earlier CSV rows without mutating the model, while allowing different records to share names or phone numbers. Duplicate feedback identifies the person's name and starting physical line number. Only when all additions succeed does it replace the model's address book with the copy and show the full directory. Consequently, invalid CSV data and identical records fail the import atomically: the current directory and active filter remain unchanged.

### Undo/redo feature
#### Implementation

The undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedAddressBook`. It extends `AddressBook` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as an `addressBookStateList` and `currentStatePointer`. A parallel `changeDescriptionList` holds the command text that led to each state, so that `undo` and `redo` can tell the user which changes they reverted or restored. Additionally, it implements the following operations:
* `VersionedAddressBook#commit(description)` — Discards any undone states, then records the current address book state and the description of the change that led to it, unless the data is unchanged.
* `VersionedAddressBook#undo()` — Reverts the most recent change by restoring an earlier state from its history, and returns that change's description.
* `VersionedAddressBook#redo()` — Restores the most recently undone state from its history, and returns that change's description.
* `VersionedAddressBook#canUndo()` and `VersionedAddressBook#canRedo()` — Return whether there is a change to revert or restore.
* `VersionedAddressBook#getUndoableCount()` and `VersionedAddressBook#getRedoableCount()` — Return how many changes can be reverted or restored one after another.

These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitAddressBook(description)`, `Model#undoAddressBook()`, `Model#redoAddressBook()`, `Model#canUndoAddressBook()`, `Model#canRedoAddressBook()`, `Model#getUndoableChangeCount()` and `Model#getRedoableChangeCount()` respectively.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.

Step 1. The user launches the application for the first time. The `VersionedAddressBook` will be initialized with the initial address book state, and the `currentStatePointer` pointing to that single address book state.
![UndoRedoState0](images/UndoRedoState0.png)

Step 2. The user executes `delete 5` command to delete the 5th person in the address book. `LogicManager` executes the command and, after the address book is saved to storage successfully, calls `Model#commitAddressBook("delete 5")` with the command text, causing the modified state of the address book to be saved in the `addressBookStateList`, and the `currentStatePointer` is shifted to the newly inserted address book state.
![UndoRedoState1](images/UndoRedoState1.png)

Step 3. The user executes `add n/David …​` to add a new person. `LogicManager` executes the command and, after a successful save, calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`, causing another modified address book state to be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.
![UndoRedoState2](images/UndoRedoState2.png)

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** No state is committed if the command fails or the save fails. If the save fails, `LogicManager` also restores the address book, the filtered list and the `currentStatePointer` to how they were before the command, so a failed `undo` leaves the history unchanged.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the person was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command calls `Model#undoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the left, pointing it to the previous address book state, and restores the address book to that state. It returns the description of the reverted change, so the result is `Undid the most recent change: add n/David …​`. The full member list is then shown.
![UndoRedoState3](images/UndoRedoState3.png)

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the initial address book state, then there is nothing to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#getUndoableChangeCount()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will show "There is no change to undo." to the user.

The following sequence diagram shows a successful `undo 2` operation through the `Logic` component. The command checks the available history before undoing either step, refreshes the full member list once, and saves once. It returns `false` from `recordsChange()`, so `LogicManager` does not commit a new history state. Model snapshots and save-failure rollback are omitted from the diagram; rollback is described in Step 3 above.
![UndoSequenceDiagram](images/UndoSequenceDiagram-Logic.png)

The following diagram expands one successful `Model#undoAddressBook()` call. `VersionedAddressBook` checks `canUndo()`, decrements `currentStatePointer`, and restores the snapshot at that index. The Logic diagram repeats this model operation once per requested step; plain `undo` uses a count of 1, as in Step 4.
![UndoSequenceDiagram](images/UndoSequenceDiagram-Model.png)

The `redo` command does the opposite: it calls `Model#redoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the address book to that state.

Both commands take an optional count, e.g. `undo 3`. `UndoCommandParser` and `RedoCommandParser` read a given count with `ParserUtil#parseCount()`, and use a count of 1 when none is given. The command first compares the count with `Model#getUndoableChangeCount()` (or `Model#getRedoableChangeCount()`). If the history is too short, it fails without changing anything, so the user is never left with only some of the requested changes undone. Otherwise it calls `Model#undoAddressBook()` (or `Model#redoAddressBook()`) once per step. `LogicManager` then saves the address book once. If that save fails, the rollback described in Step 3 restores the data and the `currentStatePointer` from before the command, so all of the steps are reverted together.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `addressBookStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest address book state, then there are no undone states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#getRedoableChangeCount()` to check if this is the case. If so, it shows "There is no undone change to redo." to the user.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. `list` does not change data, so `LogicManager` returns its result without saving or calling `Model#commitAddressBook()`. Thus, the `addressBookStateList` remains unchanged.
![UndoRedoState4](images/UndoRedoState4.png)

Step 6. The user executes `clear`. `LogicManager` executes the command and, after a successful save, calls `Model#commitAddressBook()`. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `addressBookStateList`, all address book states after the `currentStatePointer` will be purged. Reason: it no longer makes sense to redo the `add n/David …​` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** The undone states are purged even if the command leaves the data unchanged (e.g. an `edit` that sets a field to its current value), because the user sees it reported as a new change. The undone states are kept only after commands that do not save data (e.g. `list`, as in Step 5) and after `undo` and `redo` themselves, which override `Command#recordsChange()` to return `false` so that `LogicManager` does not call `Model#commitAddressBook()` after them.

#### Design considerations:
**Aspect: How undo & redo execute:**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** Saves the entire address book.
* Pros: Easy to implement.
* Cons: May have performance issues in terms of memory usage.
* **Alternative 2:** Individual command knows how to undo/redo by itself.
* Pros: Will use less memory (e.g. for `delete`, just save the person being deleted).
* Cons: We must ensure that the implementation of each individual command is correct.
**Aspect: Where states are committed:**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** `LogicManager` commits after a successful save.
* Pros: Failed saves never enter the history; new data-changing commands are undoable without extra code.

* Cons: Relies on `commit()` comparing states to skip unchanged data. The comparison uses `AddressBook#hasIdenticalData`, not `equals`, because `Instrument` and `Group` equality ignores case, which would hide a capitalisation-only edit. It also relies on `undo` and `redo` opting out through `Command#recordsChange()`.
* **Alternative 2:** Each data-changing command calls `Model#commitAddressBook()` (the original AB3 proposal).
* Pros: Explicit.
* Cons: Easy to forget in new commands; a change is recorded even if saving it fails.

### Product scope
**Target user profile**:
* is a coordinator or executive committee member of a Music CCA
* manages the records of about 50–200 members and alumni of that CCA, including both students and teachers
* deals with membership that changes frequently (e.g., new intakes each semester, members graduating to become alumni)
* often needs to find suitable players for a piece or activity based on the instruments they play and how long they have played them
* prefers desktop apps over other types of applications
* can type fast, and prefers typing to mouse interactions
* is reasonably comfortable using CLI apps

**Value proposition**: HiveMind keeps a single, searchable directory of the contact details, membership status, roles and musical experience of a Music CCA's members and alumni. It lets the coordinator shortlist players for a piece or activity (e.g., "current members who have played trumpet for at least 3 years") in a single command, faster than scanning a spreadsheet or a typical mouse-driven GUI app.
**Out of scope**: HiveMind manages the directory of one CCA only. It does not handle event registration, attendance taking, or communication and mass messaging with members.

### Non-Functional Requirements
1.  HiveMind should run on any _mainstream OS_ that has Java `25` or above installed.
2.  With a directory of up to 1,000 members, HiveMind should complete `list`, `find`, and `filter` operations within 2 seconds on a computer with a 2 GHz quad-core processor and 8 GB of RAM.
3.  A coordinator should be able to `add`, `edit`, `delete`, `list`, `find`, and `filter` operations using only the keyboard.
4.  HiveMind should display success or error feedback for each submitted command.
5.  Invalid syntax, field values, or displayed indices should produce an error explaining the rejection without changing member records.
6.  With a directories of up to 1,000 members, HiveMind should automatically save each change before reporting success, given that the local disk has sufficient free space.
### Glossary
* **Active alumnus**: An alumnus who still plays with the CCA (e.g., in alumni pieces or events).
* **Alumnus**: A former member of the CCA. An alumnus is either an _active alumnus_ or an _inactive alumnus_.
* **CCA**: Co-Curricular Activity. A student society, such as a school band or orchestra.
* **Coordinator**: The user of HiveMind, i.e., the person in the CCA who is responsible for maintaining its member records and organising players for pieces and activities.
* **Directory**: The full set of member records stored in HiveMind.

* **Displayed index**: The number shown next to a member in the list currently displayed. It may change after a `find`, `filter`, `sort` or `list`, and is used to refer to a member in commands such as `delete`.

* **Filter**: To display only members who match at least one supplied criterion in each specified field (OR within a field, AND between fields). Omitted fields impose no restriction. Unlike _find_, which searches by name only.
* **Inactive alumnus**: An alumnus who no longer plays with the CCA, but whose record is kept (e.g., for contacting them about alumni events).

* **Instrument experience**: The whole number of years a member has played a particular instrument. It is recorded separately for each instrument, and is used as the measure of a member's competency on that instrument.
* **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS.
* **Member**: A person who currently belongs to the CCA. In HiveMind, _member_ is also used loosely to mean any person in the directory, including alumni and teachers.
* **Participation group**: A group of members formed for a particular piece, activity or training programme (e.g., a group of new members under training).

* **Possible duplicate**: A person being added whose name or phone number matches that of an existing record. HiveMind warns the user but still adds the person, since two different people can share a name or a phone number.
* **Prefix**: The short label before a parameter in a command (e.g., `n/` in `n/Tan Wei Ming`) that tells HiveMind which field the value belongs to.
* **Role**: A position a person holds in the CCA (e.g., Section Leader, Conductor). Roles are free text, since each CCA names its roles differently.
* **Status**: Whether a person is a _member_, an _active alumnus_ or an _inactive alumnus_ of the CCA.
* **Type**: Whether a person is a _student_ or a _teacher_ (e.g., an instructor or teacher-in-charge) of the CCA.

## Running tests
You can run tests in two ways.

## Types of tests
This project has three types of tests:
1. *Unit tests* target the lowest-level methods and classes.
For example: `seedu.address.commons.util.StringUtilTest`
1. *Integration tests* check how multiple code units work together; the individual units are assumed to work.
For example: `seedu.address.storage.StorageManagerTest`
1. *Hybrid tests* combine unit and integration testing. These tests check both the individual units and how they work together.
For example: `seedu.address.logic.LogicManagerTest`

title: User Guide

HiveMind is a **desktop directory for Music CCA members and alumni, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). It helps coordinators view contact details, membership information, roles, and musical experience in one place. HiveMind is adapted from AddressBook Level 3 (AB3).
* Table of Contents
{:toc}
## Quick start
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Download the latest `.jar` file from the [HiveMind releases page](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T10-3/tp/releases).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for HiveMind.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar HiveMind.jar`.
HiveMind always uses the folder containing the JAR file as its _home folder_, even if you run the command from
another folder. It keeps its `data`, `imports`, and `exports` folders, preferences, and application logs inside
this home folder.

A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. On first launch without a data file, the app contains sample records. The screenshot shows these sample records; existing saved records are loaded instead if a data file is present.
![HiveMind showing member cards with contact details, type, status, optional roles, and instruments](images/Ui.png)
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `list` : Shows all members and their recorded details.
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com s/member` : Adds a current member named `John Doe`.
* `delete 3` : Deletes the 3rd contact shown in the current list.
* `clear` : Deletes all contacts.
* `exit` : Exits the app.
1. Use [Up and Down](#recalling-commands-with-arrow-keys) in the command box to recall recent submissions.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
## Empty member lists

When the directory has no members, the list area guides you to enter `add` with member details and use `help` for examples. When a search or filter has no matches in a nonempty directory, it shows **No matching members. Enter list to show everyone.** Enter `list` to restore the full directory.
## Member result count

The count above the member list shows **Showing X of Y members**: X is the number of members currently displayed and Y is the total directory size. For a directory with one member, the label uses **member**, for example **Showing 0 of 1 member** when a search has no matches. It stays visible after commands, including when `find` or `filter` displays no matches, and updates when member data changes.
## Command feedback

Command feedback has a **Success** label in green when a command completes and an **Error** label in red when it fails. Startup notices use a neutral **Information** label. Feedback wraps in narrow windows; scroll vertically in the feedback box to read longer messages, or select and copy the text.
## Features
<div markdown="block" class="alert alert-info">
**:information_source: Notes about the command format:**
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [r/ROLE]` can be used as `n/John Doe r/Section Leader` or as `n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `…`​ can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[i/INSTRUMENT:YEARS]…​` may be omitted, or written as `i/Violin:5` or `i/Violin:5 i/Piano:2`.

* Prefixed parameters can be in any order. For `export`, their order determines the CSV column order. Positional parameters must stay in the position shown in the command format; for example, `INDEX` must precede the prefixed fields in `edit`.
For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
* A parameter value cannot contain a space followed by another prefix of the same command, as HiveMind reads that as the start of a new parameter.

For example, `edit 1 r/Head g/Coach` sets the role to `Head` and the groups to `Coach`, and `edit 1 r/ n/a` removes the role and renames the person to `a`. Text such as `c/o` or `and/or` is fine, as it is not a prefix.
* Prefixes are lowercase. Prefixes from other address book apps, such as `t/` and `a/`, are not supported.
* Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.
For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
### Recalling commands with arrow keys

With the command box focused, press **↑ (Up)** to recall an older submission or **↓ (Down)** to move towards newer submissions. Recalled text is editable. **Only pressing Enter executes it**; browsing does not change members or the displayed results.
* HiveMind remembers the latest **100 nonblank submissions** in this app session, including failed commands and repeats. Closing the app clears this history.
* If you have unfinished input, Up saves it while you browse. Down after the newest submission restores that input.
* If you edit a recalled command, that edited text becomes a new draft. The next Up starts again at the newest submission; Down can restore your edited draft. Stored submissions remain unchanged.
* Up stops at the oldest available submission; Down stops at your draft. With no history, both keys leave your input unchanged.
* Use the arrow keys without Shift, Ctrl, Alt or Command/Meta. Modified arrow shortcuts keep their usual editing behaviour.
* Successful submissions still clear the command box. Failed submissions stay in the box so you can correct them.

For example, submit `list`, then `find Alex`. Type `find Ber` without pressing Enter. Up recalls `find Alex`; another Up recalls `list`. Press Down twice to return to `find Ber`, finish the command and press Enter when ready.
Command recall is separate from `undo` and `redo`: it recalls text and does not reverse changes to member records.
### Viewing help: `help`
Shows a message explaining how to access the help page.
![help message](images/helpMessage.png)
Format: `help`
### Adding a person: `add`
Adds a person to HiveMind.
Format: `add n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER e/EMAIL s/STATUS [ty/TYPE] [r/ROLE] [i/INSTRUMENT:YEARS]…​ [g/GROUP]…​`
* `s/STATUS` is required: use `member`, `active-alumnus`, or `inactive-alumnus`. Status is case-insensitive.

* `n/NAME` supports international letters and accents, numbers, ordinary spaces, apostrophes (`'` or `’`), hyphens and full stops. A name must start with a letter or number and cannot be blank. A name can contain `/` only in the markers `s/o` (son of) and `d/o` (daughter of), written between two name parts with a space on each side, as in `Ravi S/O Kumar`. For example, `Zoé Tan`, `张伟`, `Anne-Marie`, `O'Neil Tan` and `Priya d/o Raman` are accepted; `-Alex` and `Alex/Tan` are rejected.

* In a command, type `s/o` in capitals, as in `n/Ravi S/O Kumar`, because a lowercase `s/` starts the status. HiveMind stores the name exactly as you type it. A CSV import accepts the marker in any case.

* `p/PHONE_NUMBER` accepts at least three digits (`0`–`9`) with no spaces, hyphens or `+`. For example, `91234567` and `00123456789` are accepted; `12`, `ab`, `9123 4567` and `+6591234567` are rejected.

* `e/EMAIL` must have a local part, `@`, and a domain. The local part uses letters (`A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`) and digits, with single `+`, `_`, `.`, or `-` characters allowed between alphanumeric sequences. Each domain label uses letters and digits, with single hyphens allowed between alphanumeric sequences; the final label must have at least two characters. For example, `sean@example.com` and `sean.tan+cca@example-school.sg` are accepted; `not-email`, `.sean@example.com`, `sean..tan@example.com` and `sean@example.c` are rejected.

* If the name matches an existing member's name ignoring case, or the phone number matches, HiveMind shows a warning for each possible duplicate and still adds the new member. Even identical details can belong to separate records; check the warning to avoid accidental duplicates.
* `ty/TYPE` is optional: use `student` or `teacher`. It defaults to `student` when omitted.

* `r/ROLE` is optional free text, such as `Section Leader`. It cannot be blank. Extra spaces are removed, so `Vice   President`{: style="white-space: pre"} (three spaces) is saved as `Vice President` (one space).
* Type and status appear beneath the member's name on the card. If a role is supplied, it appears beneath the contact details; otherwise, the role line is hidden.
* `i/INSTRUMENT:YEARS` records an instrument the person plays and how many whole years they have played it, from `0` to `99`. For example, `i/Violin:5` or `i/Bass Guitar:1`.

* Instrument names cannot be blank or contain `:`. Each instrument can be listed only once per person; names are compared ignoring case, surrounding whitespace, and repeated whitespace, including Unicode spaces, so `Violin` and `violin` count as the same instrument. Invisible formatting characters, such as zero-width spaces copied from a web page, are removed from instrument names.

* `g/GROUP` records a participation group, such as `g/Chamber Orchestra`. It may be repeated for multiple groups. Blank group names are rejected; names are compared ignoring case, surrounding whitespace, and repeated whitespace, including Unicode spaces such as non-breaking spaces and en spaces, so repeated names are stored only once.
* Recorded groups appear in the command's success message and as separate badges on the member card. A single group called `Dance, Music` has one badge; `g/Dance g/Music` produces two badges.

* Start **each** group with the lowercase prefix `g/`, for example `g/Training g/Orchestra`. In `add`, an unrecognized prefix after a group can become part of that group's name: `g/Training gr/Orchestra` records one group named `Training gr/Orchestra`. Check the success message and correct a mistake with `edit INDEX g/Training g/Orchestra`.

The name, phone and email rules also apply when editing those fields or importing a CSV file. Spaces at the start and end of a command field are removed. Within names, repeated ordinary spaces are preserved: `Alex Tan` and `Alex  Tan` are different name spellings. The possible-duplicate name warning ignores letter case, but does not collapse those spaces.
<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-primary">:bulb: **Tip:**
A person can have any number of instruments, including zero.
Examples:
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com s/member`
* `add n/Betsy Crowe p/1234567 e/betsy@example.com s/active-alumnus ty/teacher r/Conductor i/Violin:12 i/Piano:4`
* `add n/Jane Tan p/91234567 e/jane@example.com s/member g/Chamber Orchestra g/New Member Training`
### Importing people from a CSV file: `import`
Imports people from a CSV file in the `imports` folder. The imported people are added to the existing directory; import does not replace existing people.
Format: `import FILE_NAME`
Place the CSV file in the `imports` folder inside HiveMind's home folder, then provide its file name, including the
`.csv` extension. For example, use `import members.csv` for a file named `members.csv` in that folder.
The CSV file must have this exact header and column order:
```text
name,phone,email,status,memberType,role,instruments,groups
The default `export` command produces this format. Partial exports, or exports with all eight columns in a different order,
cannot be imported. Use `export` without field selections when preparing a file for import.
Each subsequent row must have exactly these eight columns:
* `name`, `phone`, and `email` follow the same validation rules as `add`.
* `status` must be `member`, `active-alumnus`, or `inactive-alumnus`.
* `memberType` must be `student` or `teacher`.
* `role` and `groups` are optional. Represent an empty optional value with `""`.
* List multiple instruments as `NAME:YEARS` values separated by semicolons, for example `Violin:8;Piano:5`.
* List multiple groups separated by semicolons, for example `Orchestra;Leadership Team`.
* Within an instrument or group name, write `\;` for a literal semicolon and `\\` for a literal backslash. `export` applies these escapes automatically.
Example CSV file:
```csv
name,phone,email,status,memberType,role,instruments,groups
"Alicia Tan","91234567","alicia.tan@example.com","member","student","Section Leader","Violin:8;Piano:5","Orchestra;Leadership Team"
"Benjamin Lee","92345678","benjamin.lee@example.com","active-alumnus","teacher","","Cello:12",""

If any row has invalid data, does not contain eight columns, or has the same recorded details as an existing member or another CSV row, the entire import fails and the directory remains unchanged. Sharing only a name or phone number is allowed. Unlike `add`, import rejects identical records so a repeated CSV import cannot silently duplicate the directory. Instrument and group names are compared ignoring case when identifying identical records.
Example: `import members.csv`
### Listing all persons: `list`
Shows all members and alumni in the directory, in insertion order. Use this command after `find` or `filter` to return to the full list. It also clears any ordering selected with `sort`.
Format: `list`
Each member card displays:
* The member's displayed index and name in a prominent heading.

* Text badges for member type (`Student` or `Teacher`) and membership status (`Member`, `Active alumnus`, or `Inactive alumnus`). The text identifies each value without relying on colour; command inputs still use the keywords listed under `add`.
* Phone number and email address.
* A `Role:` line when a role is recorded. No role line is shown when it is absent.

* Recorded instruments and their years of experience, sorted alphabetically by instrument name, ignoring case. For example, `Piano (5 yrs)` and `Violin (1 yr)`. No instrument labels appear when none are recorded.
* A `Groups:` heading with one badge per participation group, ordered alphabetically ignoring case. No groups section is shown when none are recorded.
Long names, contact details, roles, instruments and groups wrap as the window narrows. Scroll down to see details or members below the visible area.

The same card details are shown in `find` and `filter` results. Displayed indices start at `1` and refer to the current list, so a member's index may change after a search, filter or sort. Use the current displayed index for commands such as `edit` and `delete`.
Members with matching names or contact details remain separate records. Use their current displayed indices to edit or delete the intended member.
Example: after `find alex david`, enter `list` to show everyone again. The result message is `Listed all persons.`
### Editing a person: `edit`
Edits an existing person in HiveMind.
Format: `edit INDEX [n/NAME] [p/PHONE_NUMBER] [e/EMAIL] [s/STATUS] [ty/TYPE] [r/ROLE] [i/INSTRUMENT:YEARS]…​ [g/GROUP]…​`
* Edits the person at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed person list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, …​
* At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
* Existing values will be updated to the input values.
* `s/STATUS` and `ty/TYPE` accept the same values as in `add`: `member`, `active-alumnus`, or `inactive-alumnus` for status, and `student` or `teacher` for type, ignoring case.
* `r/ROLE` replaces the person's role. To remove the role, enter `r/` without a role after it.

* If you edit the name or phone number and it then matches another member's name ignoring case, or their phone number, HiveMind shows a possible-duplicate warning for each such member, as `add` does, and still makes the edit.
* Fields that are not specified are preserved. For example, editing a person's status keeps their contact details, type, role, instruments, and groups.
* Instruments are preserved when they are not edited.
* When editing instruments, all of the person's existing instruments are replaced; adding instruments is not cumulative.
* To remove all of a person's instruments, enter `i/` without an instrument after it.
* When editing groups, all existing groups are replaced by the supplied `g/GROUP` values. To remove all groups, enter `g/` alone. Mixing an empty `g/` with named groups is invalid.
* After an edit, the full member list is shown, even if the list was showing the results of `find` or `filter`. Run the `find` or `filter` command again to return to those results.
Examples:
*  `edit 1 p/91234567 e/johndoe@example.com` Edits the phone number and email address of the 1st person to be `91234567` and `johndoe@example.com` respectively.
*  `edit 2 n/Betsy Crower i/` Edits the name of the 2nd person to be `Betsy Crower` and clears all existing instruments.
*  `edit 3 i/Cello:6 i/Piano:2` Replaces the instruments of the 3rd person with Cello (6 years) and Piano (2 years).
*  `edit 1 s/active-alumnus r/` Marks the 1st person as an active alumnus and removes their role.
*  `edit 4 ty/teacher r/Conductor` Changes the 4th person's type to teacher and their role to `Conductor`.
*  `edit 2 g/Chamber Orchestra g/Training` Replaces the 2nd person's groups.
*  `edit 2 g/` Removes all groups from the 2nd person.
### Sorting displayed members: `sort`
Orders the currently displayed members without changing which members are shown or the order saved in the data file.
Format: `sort name` or `sort status`

* `sort name` orders names alphabetically, ignoring case and treating repeated whitespace as a single space. Names are displayed and saved as entered. Names with the same comparison key retain their original directory order.
* `sort status` groups members in this order: member, active alumnus, inactive alumnus. Within each status, members retain their original directory order.
* The attribute (`name` or `status`) is case-insensitive. Exactly one attribute is required; unsupported attributes or extra arguments show the usage message.
* Sorting works on the full directory and on `find` or `filter` results, including empty results.
* Subsequent `find` and `filter` commands retain the selected ordering. Adding or editing a member also retains the ordering, while showing the full directory.
* Use the updated displayed indices for `edit` and `delete`.
* `list` restores the full directory in insertion order. Restarting also resets the ordering; the sorting preference is not saved.
Examples:
* `sort name` sorts the current results by name. The success message is `Sorted displayed members by name.`
* Run `find alex david`, then `sort status` to group the matching members by membership status. The success message is `Sorted displayed members by status.`
* Run `sort name`, then `sort status` to switch ordering. Members with the same status return to their original directory order; the previous name ordering is not used as a secondary sort.
### Locating persons by name: `find`
Finds persons whose names contain any of the given keywords, including partial words.
Format: `find KEYWORD [MORE_KEYWORDS]…`
* The search is case-insensitive; for example, `hans` matches `Hans`.
* Keyword order does not matter; for example, `Hans Bo` matches `Bo Hans`.
* The search considers only names.
* Keywords can match any part of a name; for example, `ali` and `lic` both match `Alice`.
* Persons matching at least one keyword are returned (an `OR` search); for example, `Hans Bo` returns `Hans Gruber` and `Bo Yang`.
* Matching cards retain all recorded details and are numbered from `1`. The result message reports the number of matches. If nothing matches, the list is empty.
* Use `list` to display everyone again.
Examples using the built-in sample records:
* `find ale` matches `Alex Yeoh`, demonstrating partial-name matching.
* `find alex david` matches `Alex Yeoh` and `David Li`. In the example directory below, these are the only matches, so the result is `2 person(s) listed!` with cards numbered `1` and `2`.

### Filtering persons by status, instrument, type, role, and group: `filter`
Format: `filter [s/STATUS]... [i/NAME[:MIN_YEARS]]... [ty/TYPE]... [r/ROLE]... [g/GROUP]...`
Shows people matching the specified criteria and reports the number of matches.
* At least one criterion is required. Each field is optional; an omitted field imposes no restriction.
* Introduce each member type with `ty/`: use `student` or `teacher`, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace. Repeated types use OR.
* Introduce each role with `r/`, for example `r/Section Leader`. Matches the complete role, ignoring case and extra whitespace; `r/Leader` does not match `Section Leader`. Repeated roles use OR.
* Blank or invalid types and blank roles are rejected. People without a role do not match an explicit role criterion.

* Introduce each participation group with `g/`, for example `g/Chamber Orchestra`. Matches the complete group name, ignoring case, surrounding whitespace, and repeated whitespace, including Unicode spaces such as non-breaking spaces and en spaces; `g/Orchestra` does not match `Chamber Orchestra`.

* Groups use OR: `filter g/Chamber Orchestra g/Training` matches people belonging to either group or both. Repeated names count once. Blank group names are rejected, and people without groups do not match an explicit group criterion.

* Different fields use AND: `filter ty/teacher r/Conductor s/member i/Violin:3 g/Chamber Orchestra` matches member teachers who are conductors, have at least three years on violin, and belong to Chamber Orchestra.
* Introduce each status with `s/`: use `member`, `active-alumnus`, or `inactive-alumnus`, ignoring case and surrounding whitespace.
* Statuses are combined with OR: `filter s/member s/active-alumnus` matches current members or active alumni.
* Introduce each instrument name with `i/`. `i/Violin` matches anyone who plays violin, regardless of experience.

* Optionally specify minimum years: `i/Violin:3` matches people with **at least 3 years** on violin, including exactly 3. The minimum must be a whole number from 0 to 99; blank, negative, decimal, and out-of-range values are rejected.
* Invalid minimum years, such as `filter i/Violin:abc`, report: `Minimum years should be a whole number from 0 to 99`.
* The years must belong to the matching instrument: experience on piano cannot satisfy a violin threshold.
* Instruments are combined with OR: `filter i/Violin i/Viola` matches people who play either instrument or both.

* Each repeated instrument criterion is an alternative, even for the same name: `filter i/Violin:3 i/Violin:5` matches violin players with at least 3 years. A name-only criterion such as `i/Violin` accepts any years for that instrument.

* Status and instrument groups are combined with AND: `filter s/member s/active-alumnus i/Violin:3 i/Viola:5` matches people who are members or active alumni and have at least 3 years on violin or at least 5 years on viola.

* Matches complete instrument names, ignoring case, surrounding whitespace, and repeated whitespace, including Unicode spaces such as non-breaking spaces and en spaces: `guitar` matches `Guitar`, but not `Bass Guitar`.
* Spaces after `i/` and around `:` are allowed: `filter i/ Violin : 3` is equivalent to `filter i/Violin:3`.
* Supported prefixes are `s/`, `i/`, `ty/`, `r/`, and `g/`. Unsupported member-field prefixes `n/`, `p/`, and `e/` report an error naming the prefix and listing the accepted prefixes.

* Before the first supported prefix, removed prefixes (`t/`, `a/`) and wrong-case member-field prefixes (such as `S/`) also report a prefix error. Inside values, these remain ordinary text to preserve names such as `r/Head of a/v` and `r/Student t/a`.

* Other unknown prefix-like text also remains part of the preceding value. Thus, `filter r/Lead x/1` searches for the complete role `Lead x/1`, and `filter s/member t/friend` reports an invalid status. Remove accidental text or replace it with a supported prefix.
* Searches the full directory, including after a previous `find` or `filter`.
* If no person matches, the displayed list is empty and the result reports zero matches.
* Stored records are unchanged. Use `list` to display everyone again.
Examples:
* `filter g/Chamber Orchestra`
* `filter s/member i/Violin:3 g/Chamber Orchestra`
### Exporting current results: `export`
Exports the members currently shown in the list to a CSV file.
Format: `export [f/FIELD]...`
* Without field selections, `export` writes all eight columns in this order: `name`, `phone`, `email`, `status`, `memberType`, `role`, `instruments`, `groups`.
* To choose columns, write one `f/FIELD` for each field you need. For example, `export f/name f/phone f/instruments` writes only the `name`, `phone`, and `instruments` columns, in that order.
* Select any combination of the eight field names above, using their exact spelling and case, including the capital `T` in `memberType`. Each field may be selected only once.

* Unsupported names (such as `f/address`), empty selections (`f/`), repeated selections (`f/name f/name`), and extra arguments are rejected with an error. No CSV file is created for an invalid command.

* Exports only the currently displayed members, in their displayed order. Run `find` or `filter` first to choose matching members, and `sort` to choose their order. Run `list` first to export everyone in insertion order.
* Creates a CSV file in the `exports` folder inside HiveMind’s home folder.
* Each export receives the first unused numbered filename: `current-results-01.csv`, then `current-results-02.csv`, and so on. Existing export files are not overwritten.
* Values are enclosed in double quotes. A double quote within a value is written as two double quotes.
* A member with multiple instruments or groups has them recorded in one field, separated by semicolons.
* A semicolon within an instrument or group name is escaped as `\;`, and a backslash as `\\`.
* Values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` are prefixed with a space so spreadsheet applications treat them as
text. Importing a compatible full export removes this prefix and restores the original value.
* Exporting an empty result list still creates a CSV file containing only the selected column headers, or all eight headers if no fields were selected.
* Exporting does not change member records, the displayed results, or undo/redo history.
**Import compatibility:** Partial exports cannot be imported using `import`. The importer requires all eight columns in
the default order. An export containing all eight columns in a different order is also incompatible. Use `export`
without field selections to retain the existing import-compatible format.
Examples:
* `export` exports all eight fields for the currently displayed members.
* `find alex` followed by `export f/name f/phone` exports only the names and phone numbers of members whose names contain `alex`.
* `filter s/member i/Violin` followed by `sort name`, then `export f/name f/phone f/instruments`, exports those three fields for current members who play violin, in the displayed name order.
* `export f/groups f/name` writes the `groups` column before the `name` column.
### Deleting a person: `delete`
Deletes the specified person from HiveMind.
Format: `delete INDEX`
* Deletes the person at the specified `INDEX`.
* The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed person list.
* The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, …​
Examples:
* `list` followed by `delete 2` deletes the 2nd person in the member list.
* `find Betsy` followed by `delete 1` deletes the 1st person in the results of the `find` command.
### Clearing all entries: `clear`
Clears all entries from HiveMind.
Format: `clear`
### Undoing changes: `undo`
Reverts the most recent changes made by `add`, `edit`, `delete`, `clear` or `import`.
Format: `undo [COUNT]`
* Reverts the `COUNT` most recent changes, most recent first. Without `COUNT`, only the most recent change is reverted.
* The result lists the command of each reverted change as you typed it, most recent first. For example, after `delete 1` and then `delete 3`, `undo 2` shows `delete 3`, then `delete 1`.
* `COUNT` must be a positive integer, e.g. 1, 2, 3, …​
* You can undo changes back to when HiveMind was started. If fewer than `COUNT` changes can be undone, nothing is undone and HiveMind tells you how many can be, or that there is no change to undo.
* Commands that do not change data (e.g. `list`, `find`, `filter`, `sort`, `export`) are not undone.
* An `import` is a single change, so `undo` removes everyone it added.
* After an undo, the full member list is shown.
Examples:
* `delete 2` followed by `undo` restores the deleted person.
* `delete 1`, then `delete 1` again, then `undo 2` restores both deleted people.
### Redoing undone changes: `redo`
Restores the most recent changes reverted by `undo`.
Format: `redo [COUNT]`
* Restores the `COUNT` most recently undone changes. Without `COUNT`, only the most recently undone change is restored.
* `COUNT` must be a positive integer, e.g. 1, 2, 3, …​
* Changes are restored in the reverse order of undoing: the most recently undone change comes back first.
* The result lists the command of each restored change as you typed it, in the order restored.
* If fewer than `COUNT` undone changes can be restored, nothing is redone and HiveMind tells you how many can be, or that there is no undone change to redo.

* Once you make a new change (e.g. `add`, `edit`, `delete`, `clear` or `import`) after an `undo`, the undone changes can no longer be redone. This also applies to an `edit` that leaves the member's details unchanged.
* After a redo, the full member list is shown.
Examples:
* `delete 2`, then `undo`, then `redo` deletes the person again.
* `delete 1`, then `delete 1`, then `undo 2`, then `redo` deletes only the first of the two people again.
### Exiting the program: `exit`
Exits the program.
Format: `exit`
### Saving the data
HiveMind automatically saves every successful change to member data. Commands that do not change member data, such as
`list`, `find`, `filter`, `sort`, `help`, `export` and `exit`, do not rewrite the member data file. Preferences are saved
separately when HiveMind starts and exits. You do not need to save manually.
### Editing the data file
HiveMind data is saved automatically as the JSON file `data/addressbook.json` inside HiveMind's home folder. Advanced
users are welcome to update data directly by editing that data file.
Keep an existing member's `id` unchanged when editing the data file. To create another member, use `add` so the new record receives its own ID.

When loading saved data, HiveMind ignores group entries made only of non-breaking spaces, including mixtures with ordinary spaces or tabs. Members and their other details are preserved. Empty group names and names made only of ordinary spaces or tabs make the data file invalid. Loading does not change the file; the next successful command that changes directory data saves it without the ignored group entries.
<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-warning">:exclamation: **Caution:**

If your changes make the data file invalid, HiveMind starts with an empty directory at the next run, creates a numbered backup alongside it (e.g., `addressbook.json.bak-01`, followed by `addressbook.json.bak-02` if another backup is needed), and prevents directory changes from being saved. Repair or restore the original data file before restarting the app.

Furthermore, certain edits can cause HiveMind to behave in unexpected ways (e.g., if a value entered is outside of the acceptable range). Therefore, edit the data file only if you are confident that you can update it correctly.

## FAQ
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?
**A**: Close HiveMind on both computers. Copy the `data` folder from the folder containing `HiveMind.jar` on the old
computer into the folder containing `HiveMind.jar` on the new computer. If the new installation does not have a
`data` folder yet, copy the old folder there directly; you do not need to start HiveMind first.
## Known issues

1. **When using multiple screens**, if you move the application to a secondary screen, and later switch to using only the primary screen, the GUI will open off-screen. The remedy is to delete the `preferences.json` file created by the application before running the application again.

2. **If you minimize the Help Window** and then run the `help` command (or use the `Help` menu, or the keyboard shortcut `F1`) again, the original Help Window will remain minimized, and no new Help Window will appear. The remedy is to manually restore the minimized Help Window.
3. **If `HiveMind.jar` is in a write-protected folder** (a folder where you cannot create files), HiveMind may fail
to start, or may be unable to save your changes. The remedy is to move the JAR and its home-folder contents to a
folder you can write to, such as a new folder in your user home folder.

4. **Double-clicking the JAR file may not start HiveMind**, or may start it with a different Java version, on some systems. The remedy is to start it from a terminal with `java -jar`, as described in the [Quick start](#quick-start).

5. **On macOS, if the main window is in full-screen mode**, the Help Window may open in a separate full-screen space or behind the main window. The remedy is to exit full-screen mode (e.g. press `Ctrl`+`Cmd`+`F`) before running `help`.
